correctness.rationale: For an exact ordered pair, writing g=h₁l₁ and h=h₂l₂ makes gB(g)hB(g)⁻¹=h₁h₂l₂l₁, giving the required identity. The kernel and image recover the two embedded factors. A subgroup either lies in the cyclic rotation subgroup or consists of a rotation subgroup with one coset of reflections; two rotation subgroups cannot factor the full group. In the mixed case the order-product condition is ab=n and the rotation intersection is trivial iff gcd(a,b)=1. The dihedral reflection offset runs modulo a, giving a copies in each ordering with the specified image sizes. For two reflection-bearing factors one needs 2ab=n and coprime rotation orders. A reflection lies in both factors iff their offsets agree modulo gcd(2a,2b)=2. Opposite-parity offsets give exactly n pairs, and CRT gives a single translation carrying any such pair to any other. The rotation group is characteristic for n≥3, being generated by elements of order greater than two; automorphisms have affine action on offsets, so neither factor type nor ordered sizes can be merged. This gives all orbit sizes and their counts. The parity ratio uses M_n for the mixed sector including both orderings, as specified in Proof Step 6. Then Q_n=2m·2^ω(m) and M_n=6∏(1+p^e), yielding the stated product, lower bound and probability limit. The cited odd-order theorem and explicit even nonsplitting examples justify the different scope for the full operator set.

replay.result: Direct subgroup closure, ordered product tests and map-orbit enumeration give counts 18, 36, 88. Orbit-size multisets are respectively 1 twice and 4 four times; 1,2,3 twice each and 6 four times; 1,3,4 twice each and 12 six times. The image polynomials also agree, e.g. z+8z²+8z⁴+z⁸ at n=4. The replay uses the splitting construction and does not independently test the functional identity. The uploaded verifier was not executed.

evidence: For odd n every operator splits, and the even n result permits nonsplitting maps. On D8 the example with image {1,r} has no image subgroup and is not a splitting map.

The retraction theorem classifies all idempotent endomorphisms of even dihedral groups. Inverting their outputs gives exactly the splitting maps with normal kernel: a normal H gives a projection from (G,H,L) to L, while nonnormal H cannot be an endomorphism kernel.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The retraction theorem covers a genuine subfamily after inversion (preserving images and ordinary orbits), not all splitting maps. The ordered pair with a reflection subgroup as kernel and the full rotations as image has nonnormal kernel for n≥3. The all-operator theorem does not provide the census in the relevant equivalence.

evidence: The factor-type classification supplies the permitted order partitions but not the counts of compatible embedded offsets or transitivity of affine action on ordered opposite-parity offsets.
Retraction counts transfer only to the normal-kernel subfamily and do not determine the image-size multiplicities outside it.
The odd splitting theorem transfers the resulting enumerator to all operators when n is odd, not conversely.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Recovering the weighted census still requires keeping ordered unitary decompositions, counting reflection congruence classes and proving their transitivity. Coarse class counts do not imply the exact embedded and ordinary-conjugation census; the normal-kernel subfamily formula should not be recredited if derived separately.

evidence: Splitting maps parameterize ordered embedded exact pairs, whereas the coarse factorization theorem counts unordered pairs of abstract factor isomorphism types and excludes trivial factors.
Ordinary automorphism conjugation does not exchange the ordered factors, even when alternative Rota–Baxter equivalences do.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Equivalent language for the present invariant is the weighted census of ordered embedded complements modulo common automorphism. The rough unordered equivalence is not that invariant; it cannot recover embedded multiplicities.

value.rationale: Image order and ordinary automorphism are natural invariants of these operators, and a rough list of abstract factor types loses precisely the multiplicities needed for them. The full census exposes an even-order family with orbit size n and quantifies when it dominates, not just which factor types occur. The result gives exact usable data for every dihedral group and for all operators in the odd case, rather than another small-order table.
